## Abstract

Dengue arises from coupled interactions among mosquitoes, viruses, human hosts,
environments, and systems of observation. This hypothesis-driven ecological
perspective uses a certified reproducible descriptive analysis of official
Argentine surveillance data as its empirical basis. It is not a new
epidemiological study, causal analysis, climate-attribution study, transmission
model, or incidence study. In SE31/2024--SE30/2025, the analysis retained
17,844 published counts. The observed national maximum was at season week 36,
the weighted temporal center was 35.76 weeks, and the shortest windows
containing 50%, 80%, and 90% of published counts lasted 5, 10, and 12 weeks.
Regional timing differed, and NEA had a tied rather than unique peak. In
calendar year 2024, population adjustment reordered provinces: Buenos Aires
was first by published count but sixteenth by published-count rate per 100,000,
while Tucumán moved from third to first.

These patterns are consistent with, but do not demonstrate, a seasonally forced
vector--virus--host system. The proposed framework separates a latent biological
process--linking climate and habitat, mosquito population dynamics,
vector--virus biology, and human hosts--from the observation process through
which transmission becomes healthcare seeking, detection, notification,
classification, geographic assignment, and a published dataset. It explains why
population size, habitat, mobility, immunity, serotypes, and surveillance can
all shape observed heterogeneity, offers five falsifiable predictions, and
specifies independent data required to test them. Published counts remain
neither unique people, incidence, individual risk, nor direct measurements of
transmission.

**Keywords:** Dengue; *Aedes aegypti*; population ecology; vector ecology;
seasonal dynamics; surveillance; Argentina; spatial heterogeneity.

## Resumen en español {.unnumbered}

Este artículo presenta una interpretación ecológica orientada por hipótesis de
patrones descriptivos certificados de vigilancia de dengue en Argentina. No es
un nuevo estudio epidemiológico ni una demostración causal. Para la temporada
SE31/2024--SE30/2025, el análisis reproducible de datos oficiales publicados
retuvo 17.844 conteos publicados; el máximo nacional observado fue la semana
estacional 36 y la concentración temporal fue marcada. Los descriptores
regionales fueron heterogéneos; en NEA el máximo fue un empate y no una semana
única. Para el año calendario 2024, el ajuste por población reordenó los
territorios: Buenos Aires pasó del primer lugar por conteo publicado al
decimosexto por tasa de conteos publicados por 100.000, mientras Tucumán pasó
del tercero al primero.

La hipótesis considera un sistema estacional vector--virus--huésped. Distingue
el proceso biológico latente --hábitat, dinámica de *Aedes aegypti*, biología
vector--virus y población humana-- del proceso de observación mediante el cual
la transmisión puede llegar a atención sanitaria, detección, notificación,
clasificación, asignación geográfica y datos publicados. La contribución es
conceptual: los patrones son compatibles con mecanismos ecológicos, pero no los
demuestran. Se proponen predicciones falsables y la evidencia independiente que
sería necesaria para evaluarlas. Los conteos publicados no son personas únicas,
incidencia ni riesgo individual.

# Introduction

Dengue is a coupled vector--virus--host--environment system, not simply a time
series of reported disease. Temperature and its daily variation can affect
mosquito development, survival, reproduction, infection, and extrinsic
incubation, often nonlinearly [@mordecai2019; @lambrechts2011;
@carrington2013life]. Habitat and urban form determine where mosquitoes can
persist; human population distribution and daily movement shape vector--host
contact; and immunity and circulating serotypes alter the susceptible host
population.

Argentina is informative because it spans heterogeneous climatic and ecological
environments. Field work in Buenos Aires, Córdoba, the Northwest, and the
Northeast documents seasonal and spatial variation in *Aedes aegypti* abundance
or oviposition, and the importance of temperature, weather, microhabitat, and
urban conditions [@vezzani2004; @demajo2013; @benitez2021; @estallo2015;
@gimenez2020; @vezzani2005; @montini2021]. Evidence of long-term vector dynamics and range expansion makes
ecological interpretation relevant, but does not make climate sufficient to
explain a particular surveillance pattern [@fischer2017; @rubio2020].

This article interprets the completed *Argentina Dengue Surveillance* project,
a reproducible contract-first descriptive analysis of official public releases.
Its certified report is available [online](https://etalii.github.io/scientific-data-portfolio/argentina-dengue-analysis/).
The project distinguishes absolute published counts from published-count rates
per 100,000. Population size can contribute to an absolute numerator, while
population adjustment can reveal that population size alone does not summarize
territorial heterogeneity. It does not turn reported counts into incidence,
individual risk, infection probability, or a direct measurement of transmission
intensity.

Our objective is to formulate an ecological hypothesis that organizes the
certified descriptive patterns, identifies competing explanations, and
specifies independent evidence needed to test them. We do not claim that the
surveillance analysis tests the hypothesis.

# Empirical basis and analytical boundaries

The project consumes official Argentine surveillance releases and, for
calendar-year geographic displays, official INDEC population denominators. It
produces a reproducible description of published counts, published-count rates
per 100,000, documented geographic assignment, and observed temporal
descriptors. It does not identify people, deduplicate epidemiological cases, or
estimate latent infections.

Two scopes are intentionally non-interchangeable. The seasonal scope,
SE31/2024--SE30/2025, contains 17,844 published counts. Its observed national
maximum is season week 36; its weighted temporal center is 35.76356 and its
weighted median is week 36. The shortest contiguous observed windows reaching
50%, 80%, and 90% of the total are 5, 10, and 12 weeks. It retains 678
published counts with unknown or nonassignable geography, and geographic mapping
completeness is 96.2%. This describes assignment within scope, not surveillance
completeness.

The geographic comparison uses calendar year 2024 and a contemporary
denominator scenario. Its territorial numerators include only geographically
mapped published counts; 27,220 national published counts lack provincial
geography and are not redistributed. A published-count rate per 100,000 is not
incidence, an attack rate, individual risk, or a complete territorial numerator.
No cumulative cross-year seasonal rate is reported.

The data do not support claims about unique people, transmission chains,
epidemic propagation, causal effects, or unobserved regional zeros. Missing
region-week rows remain missing rather than zero-filled. They also do not
support direct epidemiological comparison of annual totals for 2018, 2022,
2024, and 2025, or age-specific rates. These observations are the endpoint of a
surveillance process, not direct measurements of the biological system that
generated infections.

# Ecological hypothesis and testable predictions

## Central hypothesis

The temporal concentration and geographic heterogeneity of published dengue
counts in Argentina are consistent with a seasonally forced vector--virus--host
system. In this hypothesis, local transmission potential can increase when
*Aedes aegypti* population dynamics and temperature-dependent vector--virus
processes encounter favourable seasonal conditions within particular human and
urban settings. Human population size contributes importantly to absolute
published counts. Habitat, human--vector contact, mobility, viral introduction,
host susceptibility, serotype circulation, and the observation process can all
modify population-adjusted published patterns.

This is a hypothesis about a latent system. The certified findings are
compatible with it, but do not identify its parameters or demonstrate a
mechanism. Climate, mosquito abundance, mobility, immunity, serotypes, and
healthcare use were not measured in the analysis and must not be inferred from
the reported patterns.

## Falsifiable predictions

The following predictions are deliberately framed so that independent evidence
could weaken as well as support the ecological hypothesis.

1. **Seasonal vector suitability.** If seasonal vector ecology is important,
   measured adult or immature mosquito abundance, or a pre-specified
   climate-derived suitability measure, should systematically precede or overlap
   the surveillance rise with biologically plausible lags. Weekly mosquito
   surveillance and weather data, linked at compatible places and times, are
   required. Repeated strong surveillance peaks during periods of low measured
   vector suitability would weaken this component of the hypothesis.
2. **Population size and territorial reordering.** If population size explains
   only part of the spatial pattern, absolute published counts should relate
   strongly to population size while population-adjusted published patterns
   retain structured heterogeneity associated with independently measured
   ecological or contact conditions. Comparable population, habitat,
   entomological, and mobility data are required. If adjusted patterns show no
   reproducible heterogeneity once measurement quality is assessed, this
   prediction would be weakened.
3. **Regional seasonal heterogeneity.** If differing local seasonal conditions
   matter, regional timing should covary with independently measured thermal
   regimes, habitat, or vector phenology rather than simply reflecting a common
   schedule. Harmonized region-week entomological and environmental series are
   required. Stable identical timing across ecologically contrasting regions,
   after comparable observation, would weaken this prediction.
4. **Introductions and connectivity.** If mobility and viral introduction are
   important, changes in local surveillance patterns should align with
   independently documented travel, importation, or viral-lineage evidence in
   receptive vector populations. Travel histories, mobility measures, and
   genomic surveillance are required. Strong local pulses repeatedly occurring
   without compatible introduction or connectivity evidence would weaken this
   explanation.
5. **Host susceptibility and serotypes.** If susceptible fraction and serotype
   circulation modify epidemic magnitude, otherwise similar vector and habitat
   settings should differ in their published patterns in ways that correspond to
   independent seroprevalence and virological data. Longitudinal serological and
   serotype surveillance are required. Consistent magnitude despite sharply
   different measured susceptibility or serotype conditions would weaken this
   component.

These predictions are not tested here. They also are not mutually exclusive:
support for one would not eliminate the need to evaluate the others or the
observation process.

# Two-process conceptual framework

The central conceptual contribution is to separate what is biologically latent
from what is observed administratively. The observed surveillance signal is the
joint product of an underlying biological system and an observation process.
The first process concerns conditions under which infections may occur; the
second concerns how some resulting events become published records.

```{mermaid}
flowchart TB
  subgraph latent[Latent biological process]
    C[Climate and habitat] --> M[Aedes aegypti population dynamics]
    M --> V[Vector-virus processes]
    V --> H[Human host population]
    H --> T[Transmission]
    U[Urban habitat] --> M
    U --> H
    X[Human mobility] --> H
    X --> T
    I[Host immunity] --> H
    S[Serotype circulation] --> H
    S --> V
  end
  subgraph observation[Observation process]
    T --> D[Healthcare seeking and detection]
    D --> N[Notification]
    N --> CL[Classification]
    CL --> G[Geographic assignment]
    G --> P[Published surveillance dataset]
  end
```

**Figure 1. Conceptual framework.** The upper process represents hypothesized
biological relationships; the lower process represents the pathway through
which transmission may become a published surveillance record. This is not an
estimated causal model.

The latent process includes mosquito recruitment, immature development, adult
survival, oviposition, biting, infection, extrinsic incubation, and survival to
infectiousness. It also includes the size and structure of human populations,
their contact with vectors, mobility, immunity, and circulating serotypes.
The observation process includes healthcare contact, detection, notification,
classification, and geographic assignment. The certified project directly
analyzes the endpoint of the second process, not the latent biological process
itself.

This distinction is useful as a cautious *ecology of observation*: the ability
to infer biological dynamics depends on how biological events pass through
healthcare contact and institutional recording. It does not presume the
magnitude or direction of any under-ascertainment in this dataset. Rather, it
requires that differences among published signals be interpreted as potentially
shaped by both systems until appropriate independent evidence is available.

# Biological interpretation of certified patterns

## Seasonal concentration

The certified season has a concentrated national published-count profile: half
of its total falls within the shortest five-week observed window, 80% within ten
weeks, and 90% within twelve weeks. Its observed maximum and weighted median
both occur at season week 36, while its weighted temporal center is
approximately 35.76. A concentrated pulse is biologically compatible with a
seasonally forced vector--host system: recruitment and development of immature
mosquitoes, seasonal adult survival, oviposition, biting, and
temperature-dependent vector--virus processes can overlap with changing human
exposure during a limited interval. Seasonal patterns of *Ae. aegypti*
abundance and oviposition in Argentina make that interpretation biologically
plausible [@vezzani2004; @fischer2017; @estallo2015].

Compatibility is not attribution. The curve contains published counts, not
temperature, rainfall, entomological abundance, infection onset, human movement,
or viral-introduction data. It cannot establish that temperature, mosquito
abundance, or rainfall caused the week-36 maximum; infer a lag; or estimate
vectorial capacity. The concentration windows summarize observations in the
configured scope. They do not define true epidemic duration or the duration of
latent transmission.

![National seasonal profile of published counts for SE31/2024--SE30/2025. It
retains unknown or nonassignable geography, identifies the observed peak at
SE36, and displays certified concentration descriptors.](../figures/season_national_temporal_profile_en.png){#fig-season-national}

**Figure 2.** National published-count profile in the configured season. It
describes published observations, not complete surveillance or latent
transmission.

## Regional observed timing

Regional descriptors differ across observed region weeks. Centro's unique peak
is at season week 36, Cuyo's at 32, NOA's at 33, and Sur's at 34; NEA has a tie
at weeks 17 and 38. That tie prevents selection of an arbitrary single NEA
peak. Observed regional-week coverage also varies from 18 weeks in Sur to 52 in
NEA.

The heterogeneity is compatible with regional variation in thermal regimes,
urban habitat, vector population dynamics, mobility, introductions, and host
susceptibility. Each is a hypothesis, not an interpretation established by the
figure. In particular, the descriptors do not show geographic propagation or
identify a route between regions. Missing region-week rows are not zero-filled,
so the absence of a row cannot be read as absence of dengue, transmission, or
reporting.

![Observed regional timing descriptors for published counts in
SE31/2024--SE30/2025. NEA has a tied observed peak, and missing region-week
rows are not treated as zero.](../figures/season_regional_observed_timing_en.png){#fig-season-region}

**Figure 3.** Regional observed timing descriptors, using observed region weeks
only and preserving the NEA peak tie.

## Absolute counts and population-adjusted patterns

In calendar-year 2024, Buenos Aires ranks first by published count and
sixteenth by published-count rate per 100,000. Tucumán moves from third to
first, La Rioja from twelfth to second, and Catamarca from thirteenth to fourth.
These rank shifts show that population size and population-adjusted published
counts answer different descriptive questions. A large population can
contribute to a large numerator. A smaller population can yield a higher
published-count rate without establishing greater individual risk or a higher
true transmission level.

The result is compatible with heterogeneous ecological and social conditions,
but it does not measure ecological suitability. Urban habitat, human--vector
contact, vector abundance, mobility or introductions, immunity, serotypes, and
reporting may all contribute to the ordering after population adjustment. The
strongest inference is therefore descriptive: population size alone does not
summarize territorial published patterns. The rank shifts do not identify which
process is responsible, and provincial numerators exclude unknown or
nonassignable geography.

![Provincial rank shifts between published count and published-count rate per
100,000 in calendar year 2024. Territorial numerators exclude unknown or
nonassignable geography and the rate is not incidence or individual risk.](../figures/province_count_rate_rank_shift_2024_en.png){#fig-province-ranks}

**Figure 4.** Population adjustment changes provincial ordering in calendar year
2024 under the contemporary denominator scenario.

## Regional contrast

Centro has the largest geographically mapped regional published count, whereas
NOA has the largest regional published-count rate per 100,000. This parallel
with the provincial rank shifts is consistent with the premise that population
structure and ecological heterogeneity can contribute differently to absolute
and population-adjusted patterns. It does not establish a regional ecological
gradient: territorial numerators exclude unknown or nonassignable geography,
and neither regional rate measures incidence nor attributes a biological
mechanism.

# Discussion

## Seasonal forcing and mosquito population ecology

*Aedes aegypti* populations are not static. Recruitment depends on eggs entering
available breeding sites; immature development and mortality depend on local
temperature and water conditions; adults must survive, obtain blood meals, and
oviposit to sustain future cohorts. Container availability, water storage,
rainfall, household practices, and built environments can alter this sequence
locally. Seasonal population growth or decline consequently reflects a chain of
life-history processes rather than a single environmental variable. In Buenos
Aires, vector activity and infestation vary substantially across the year
[@vezzani2004], while microclimatic heterogeneity can create short-distance
differences [@demajo2013]. In Orán and Córdoba, oviposition has been associated
with weather and environmental variables with context-specific lags
[@estallo2015; @benitez2021].

This biology matters because adult abundance can affect the opportunity for
human--vector contact, but abundance alone is not a sufficient measure of
transmission potential. A large mosquito population may coexist with limited
viral introduction, lower vector infection, reduced survival through the
extrinsic incubation interval, a small susceptible fraction, or a surveillance
signal that does not mirror all infections. Conversely, a modest abundance at a
critical time may still contribute to observed transmission when other
conditions align. The manuscript therefore treats mosquito population dynamics
as one component of a coupled system, not as a direct proxy for published
counts.

Precipitation is especially unsuitable for a universal account: its effects can
depend on container types, water management, rainfall intensity, and locality.
The appropriate language is “consistent with,” “may modify,” and “requires
direct measurement,” rather than climate determinism. Argentine national-scale
work likewise frames climate alongside demographic and regional processes rather
than as a solitary determinant [@carbajo2018; @lopez2023].

## From mosquito abundance to transmission potential

Vectorial capacity is a useful conceptual bridge between mosquito population
dynamics and transmission, not an estimated quantity in this project. It
depends on more than abundance: biting and contact, survival, infection and
vector competence, the duration of extrinsic incubation, and survival long
enough to become infectious all matter. Temperature can affect several of these
traits nonlinearly, and the trait that limits transmission can differ across
thermal conditions [@mordecai2019]. Daily thermal fluctuation can alter mosquito
survival and competence, so mean temperature alone can obscure relevant
biological variation [@lambrechts2011; @carrington2013life;
@carrington2013extreme].

The certified surveillance profile cannot distinguish a pulse produced by
seasonal mosquito demography from one shaped principally by introductions, host
susceptibility, or observation. A future evaluation would need linked
meteorological series, measures of immature and adult vectors, virus detection
or competence evidence, and an explicitly specified observation model. Such a
design could ask whether changes in vector-related conditions consistently
precede the published signal, rather than retrospectively assigning the observed
peak to a single driver.

## Human populations as ecological components

Human populations are more than denominators. Their size can affect absolute
published counts, but the susceptible fraction, previous exposure,
serotype-specific immunity, movement, daily activity, housing, and patterns of
human--vector contact can modify epidemic magnitude under superficially similar
environmental conditions. A receptive vector population does not by itself imply
the same opportunity for viral introduction, amplification, or observation in
every place.

Argentine serological studies demonstrate that antibody prevalence and serotype
information can be measured independently and can vary geographically
[@flichman2022; @macchia2025; @biscayart2025]. These studies do not identify the
immunity or serotype histories of the people represented in the certified
artifacts. No individual serostatus, serotype, genomic lineage, or
prior-infection history is present here. Host immunity and serotypes therefore
remain alternative explanations and future measurement targets, not
retrospective explanations for the reported peak or rank shifts.

## Spatial heterogeneity, habitat, and contact

The provincial and regional rank shifts make a narrow but important point:
population size does not exhaust the information in territorial published
counts. Urban form, housing, water storage, container habitat, socioeconomic
conditions, and human--vector contact can create local contrasts in mosquito
habitat and exposure. In Buenos Aires, travel, housing, and socioeconomic
conditions were relevant to heterogeneous local dengue transmission during the
2016 event [@gurevitz2021]. Northern Argentine studies also document spatially
structured and temporally unstable mosquito habitat patterns [@garelli2013;
@espinosa2016].

This evidence supports a plausible mechanism at its own geographic and
measurement scales. It does not translate a high published-count rate into
suitability, nor does it establish that La Rioja, Catamarca, Tucumán, or NOA
had any particular ecological condition in the certified scope. Instead, the
rank shifts motivate the testable expectation that appropriately measured
ecological and social conditions could account for variation beyond population
size. That expectation requires compatible-scale data and explicit treatment of
the observation process.

## Mobility and viral introductions

Human movement can couple territories by moving infected people between places
with different vector and host conditions. Travel was part of the Buenos Aires
analysis [@gurevitz2021], and mobility is a recognized explanatory mechanism in
dengue research and infectious-disease synthesis [@stoddard2013; @lessani2024].
An introduction into a receptive vector and host setting could help generate a
local pulse even when local environmental suitability is similar to that of a
place without a documented introduction.

A metapopulation analogy is useful conceptually, but the regional timing figure
does not document routes of spread. Mobility and importation compete with a
purely local ecological explanation and can also operate alongside it. Travel
histories, commuting or mobility measures, virus genomes, and data on likely
introduction events would be needed to distinguish these pathways. The
descriptive timing differences should not be described as geographic
propagation.

## Competing explanations

The ecological hypothesis must be evaluated against explanations that can
produce part of the same certified patterns. First, a demographic explanation
expects population size to contribute strongly to absolute counts; the
population-adjusted rank shifts show only that it is not the entire descriptive
story. Population data paired with like-for-like territorial numerators would
clarify its contribution. Second, mobility and viral introductions can shape the
timing and magnitude of local events; travel, genomic, and importation evidence
would help distinguish this from locally generated variation. Third, urban
habitat, housing, water-storage practices, and socioeconomic heterogeneity can
alter breeding opportunities and contact; fine-scale entomological and social
measurements would be needed to assess that mechanism.

Fourth, immunity, susceptible fraction, and serotype circulation can modify the
human host component even under similar vector conditions; serial
seroprevalence and virological surveillance would be needed to evaluate this
possibility. Fifth, the surveillance and reporting process can modify which
biological events become published records. These processes are not mutually
exclusive. No observed rank, peak, or concentration window is uniquely
diagnostic of one of them.

## Surveillance as an observation process

Surveillance is not merely a caveat; it conditions inference. Reporting delays,
healthcare seeking, detection, laboratory capacity, definitions,
classification, notification, geographic assignment, and publication can each
shape the endpoint that is observed. Dengue surveillance literature documents
variation in ascertainment and operational performance [@runge2014;
@susong2026]. Argentine and regional guidance establish detection,
notification, and classification as distinct institutional stages
[@argentina2025; @paho2023]. Regional systematic-review evidence likewise
emphasizes heterogeneity in dengue surveillance and interpretation
[@torres2017].

The certified project preserves unknown geography, does not complete missing
regional weeks, and retains source duplicate/conflict evidence rather than
silently resolving it. It lacks individual identifiers and analyzes published
counts rather than known unique cases. These properties make the two-process
framework practically important: a published surveillance pattern can differ
from a biological transmission pattern because the observation process has its
own structure. This does not mean every difference is surveillance bias or
reporting artefact, and it does not estimate under-ascertainment. It means that
biological interpretation must remain conditional on evidence about both
processes.

## Why annual snapshots do not establish ecological trends

This article does not infer climate-change trends, vector adaptation, increasing
transmission, or epidemic growth from the 2018, 2022, 2024, and 2025 annual
snapshots. The certified project considers direct annual/interannual comparison
unsupported because coverage, schemas, semantic evidence, and observation
conditions differ. External literature may motivate hypotheses about climatic
suitability or range dynamics [@fischer2017; @lopez2023], but cannot convert
these four snapshots into a within-project trend analysis.

## What evidence would test the hypothesis

The five predictions define the minimum evidence needed for a future evaluation.
Weekly meteorological series and repeated immature and adult mosquito measures
would be needed to assess temporal suitability and population dynamics.
Comparable habitat, land-cover, housing, water-storage, contact, and population
data would be needed to evaluate spatial heterogeneity. Travel, commuting,
importation, and viral genomic data would be needed to assess connectivity and
introductions. Seroprevalence, serotype, and longitudinal immunity data would be
needed to assess the host component. Finally, any inferential design needs an
observation component covering healthcare contact, detection, notification,
classification, and geographic assignment.

These additions would enable pre-specified tests that can fail as well as
succeed. They would not eliminate uncertainty automatically, but they would
separate an ecological explanation from demographic, mobility, immunity, and
surveillance alternatives more rigorously than descriptive surveillance patterns
alone can do.

# Conclusions

The certified analysis identifies a concentrated seasonal pulse of published
counts and substantial spatial heterogeneity in the relationship between
absolute and population-adjusted published counts. These patterns are
biologically consistent with a seasonally forced vector--virus--host system,
but they do not resolve the mechanisms that generated them. Population size is
consequential for absolute counts, yet rank shifts show why it is not the sole
descriptive component of territorial heterogeneity.

The central conclusion is deliberately limited: a published surveillance
dataset is the endpoint of an observation process, not a direct view of latent
transmission. Treating the observed signal as the joint product of biological
and observation processes preserves the value of reproducible descriptive
evidence while avoiding causal claims it cannot support. Independent
entomological, environmental, mobility, virological, serological, and
surveillance-process data are required to test the hypothesis.
